comparisons.peer_summary: Intel launched Intel Xeon 6 processors for data centers using Intel 3 process and Efficient cores, designed to address diverse workload deployments. The 5th Gen Intel Xeon Scalable processors, based on Intel 7, continued to ramp throughout 2024.
comparisons.comparison: Both AMD and Intel disclose specific launches of server CPU families aimed at data center workloads during fiscal 2024. AMD highlights the announcement of its 5th generation EPYC family, focusing on expanding its high-performance server CPU portfolio based on x86 architecture. Similarly, Intel details the launch of its Intel Xeon 6 processors for the data center, noting the use of its Intel 3 process and Efficient cores to address diverse workload deployments. While both companies focus on new server CPU generations for data centers, AMD emphasizes the expansion of its existing EPYC lineage, whereas Intel distinguishes its new Xeon 6 launch with specific process technology (Intel 3) and core architecture (E-cores) compared to its previously launched 5th Gen Scalable processors.

sentences.text: We recently announced our 5th generation AMD EPYC family of server processors, further expanding our high-performance server CPU portfolio.

▪Data center CPUs. We launched our Intel® Xeon® 6 processors for the data center, utilizing the Intel 3 process, including our first Intel Xeon processor using Efficient cores (E-cores). The Intel Xeon 6 family is designed to address the growing diversity in workloads and deployments in the data center environments. Our 5th Gen Intel Xeon Scalable processors, based on Intel 7, were launched in 2023, and continued to ramp throughout 2024.

comparisons.peer_summary: Compute offerings include supercomputing platforms and servers integrating GPUs, DPUs, interconnects, and AI/HPC software stacks, along with NVIDIA AI Enterprise software, DGX Cloud, and various libraries, APIs, SDKs, and frameworks.
comparisons.comparison: The target disclosure focuses on AMD's server CPUs (EPYC) designed for high-performance computing and data centers. NVIDIA discloses its compute offerings which include supercomputing platforms and servers that bring together GPUs, DPUs, and fully optimized AI and HPC software stacks. While AMD's item 1 disclosure centers on the CPU component of server computing, NVIDIA's related disclosure highlights a broader compute platform integrating GPUs and software for the same HPC and AI data center markets. The similarity lies in the shared end-market focus (AI/HPC data centers), but the difference is in the core hardware technology disclosed: x86 server processors (AMD) versus GPU-accelerated computing platforms (NVIDIA).
